name: Ludwig Museum
description: Hungary's museum of contemporary art with an international outlook grew from works donated by the collectors Peter and Irene Ludwig. It now occupies the Danube-facing wing of Müpa Budapest, where Hungarian and Eastern European art hangs alongside Western pop art, and it also runs Hungary's pavilion at the Venice Biennale.

children.text: The Ludwig Museum – Museum of Contemporary Art is housed in the Danube-facing wing of Müpa Budapest, the arts complex in Ferencváros beside the Rákóczi bridge. The museum describes itself as the only museum of contemporary art in Hungary that collects international art, and its 2005 move into the Müpa gave it around 3,300 square metres of exhibition space spread over three storeys.

The story begins with the German collector Peter Ludwig, who trained as a lawyer and art historian and ran a chocolate business. In 1983 the exhibition Universal Art since 1960 came to the Kunsthalle in Budapest from Vienna and drew more than 40,000 visitors in four months; it was then that the idea of a Ludwig museum in the city was first raised. The founding contract was signed in Budapest on 21 March 1989, with 70 works donated to the Hungarian state, and a further 91 works were placed on long-term deposit in 1991. The first permanent exhibition opened in Building A of the Buda Palace on 4 June 1991.

Katalin Néray directed the museum from 1993 until her death in 2007, and under her leadership it built up a programme of temporary exhibitions that began in the palace and counted more than 200 between 1991 and 2007. Peter Ludwig died on 22 July 1996, and Irene Ludwig then helped set up the Peter and Irene Ludwig Foundation. The decision to leave the palace was taken in 2003, and the Palace of Arts, which officially opened on 14 March 2005, became the museum's new home that year.

What makes the collection unusual is Peter Ludwig's stated aim of bringing together the art of the ideologically divided world before 1989. The museum therefore shows Hungarian and Eastern European work next to Western pieces. The museum names Warhol, Lichtenstein and Oldenburg among the American and British pop artists whose emblematic works the Ludwigs brought to Budapest, and Hungarian artists such as László Lakner, Dóra Maurer and Ilona Keserü among its holdings. Since the 1990s it has also collected systematically from the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Poland, Romania and Slovenia, including Roman Ondák, Zbigniew Libera and Dan Perjovschi.

One detail the museum itself highlights is that it holds the first NFT work acquired by a Hungarian museum, a network piece called New Songs of New Times, or Art as Data by the BarabásiLab group led by Albert-László Barabási. The museum also manages the Hungarian Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, and its director serves as national commissioner.
Good to know
Müpa Budapest stands near the Rákóczi bridge, next to the National Theatre; the H6 and H7 suburban railway is listed as a rail connection to the complex.
Exhibitions change, so check the museum's official site for current shows, opening times and tickets before you go.
The museum's website lists a museum shop, a library and accessibility information, which is worth reading if you have particular needs.
Müpa Budapest also has its own concert hall and Festival Theatre in the same building, so it can be combined with an evening performance.

historyIntro: The Ludwig Museum reflects Budapest's place in modern European art, particularly the exchange between Central European and international ideas.

historySections.heading: A collection looking beyond national borders

children.text: The museum is named for the Ludwig art-collecting tradition and focuses on modern and contemporary works. Hungarian and international artists are placed in conversation rather than separated into unrelated histories.

Located in the Müpa cultural complex, the museum uses exhibitions and educational programmes to explore art made in changing social and political settings. Its content evolves, which makes the building a different experience across visits.

name: Kunsthalle
description: Műcsarnok, also called the Kunsthalle, faces the Museum of Fine Arts across Heroes' Square. Built for the 1896 millennium celebrations, it follows the German Kunsthalle model: no permanent collection, just changing exhibitions of contemporary art. It is the largest exhibition space for contemporary visual art in Hungary.

children.text: Műcsarnok, which translates roughly as art hall, is Budapest's Kunsthalle. It stands on Heroes' Square at Dózsa György út 37, facing the Museum of Fine Arts. It follows the pattern of the German Kunsthalle: it keeps no collection of its own, is run by artists and stages temporary exhibitions, with Wikipedia calling it the largest exhibition space for contemporary visual art in Hungary. It is an institution of the Hungarian Academy of Arts.

The institution is older than the building you see today. It was founded in 1877 on the initiative of the Hungarian National Fine Arts Association and first occupied a building at 69–71 Andrássy Avenue, a site that now belongs to the Hungarian University of Fine Arts. The Heroes' Square building was erected in 1896 for the millennium celebrations, and the institution describes itself as the home of Hungarian visual art since that year. Wikipedia credits the design to Albert Schickedanz and Fülöp Herczog, while the institution's own history page names Schickedanz alone.

The architecture is Neoclassical, with a Greek Revival portico at the front. Behind it a three-bayed, semi-circular apse houses a roofed exhibition hall that receives light through skylights. The building was renovated in 1995, and since then it has hosted leading Hungarian and international contemporary artists. A bookshop, a library and a café overlooking the square are also part of the complex, and the institution runs an archive, workshops and an online time machine devoted to its past.

Because there is no permanent display, what you see depends entirely on the current programme. The institution's own site has marked its 130th anniversary with a jubilee exhibition called Műcsarnok 130. The Kunsthalle has also played a part in the story of other Budapest museums: in 1983 the exhibition Universal Art since 1960 came here from Vienna, and its success prompted talks about a contemporary art museum in Budapest.
Good to know
Heroes' Square is the stop on the Millennium Underground (the M1 line); the Műcsarnok site also lists trolleybus and bus connections.
Check the official Műcsarnok site for the current exhibitions, opening times and tickets, as the programme changes regularly.
The Museum of Fine Arts is directly opposite and the Museum of Ethnography is at Dózsa György út 35, so the area works well for a day of museums.
The building has a café overlooking the square, which is useful for a break between exhibitions.

historyIntro: Kunsthalle, the large exhibition hall on Heroes' Square, represents Budapest's changing art scene rather than a fixed museum collection.

historySections.heading: An exhibition venue facing Heroes' Square

children.text: The building is part of the monumental cultural setting created around the city's millennium-era development. Its prominent entrance faces the square and complements the Museum of Fine Arts opposite.

historySections.heading: Art that changes with the programme

children.text: Unlike a collection-based museum, Kunsthalle focuses on rotating exhibitions of contemporary Hungarian and international art. The history visitors encounter here is therefore also the history of new artistic ideas as they are presented.

name: Gellért Thermal Bath
description: The Gellért Thermal Bath is Budapest's Art Nouveau bath beside the Danube at the foot of Gellért Hill. Built in 1912–1918 with the Hotel Gellért, it is currently reported closed for refurbishment, so check the operator's notice before planning a visit.

children.text: The Gellért Thermal Bath belongs to the Hotel Gellért, on the Buda bank next to the Liberty Bridge. It was built between 1912 and 1918 in the Secession (Art Nouveau) style, and both the bath and the hotel opened in 1918. The main hall, with its gallery and glass roof, and the mosaic-tiled thermal pools are among the city's best-known interiors.

The site has a long bathing history. References to healing waters here go back to the 13th century, a hospital stood on the site in the Middle Ages, and baths were built under Ottoman rule. The old name, Sárosfürdő, 'muddy bath', recalls the mineral mud that settled at the bottom of the pools. The water, at about 35–40 °C, contains calcium, magnesium, hydrocarbonate and other minerals.

The complex was extended in 1927 with an outdoor artificial wave pool, and in 1934 a thermal bath under a glass dome was installed in the hotel's former winter garden. Near the end of World War II the bath's Art Nouveau women's section was bombed, destroying its pyrogranite facade and wooden dressing rooms, and the post-war repairs were plainer. All pools became mixed-gender in 2013.

Important for planning: the bath is reported to have closed in October 2025 for a long refurbishment, with reopening planned for 2028. Because dates like these can change, check the operator's official website for the current status before you build a visit around it. Budapest has other thermal baths in the meantime, including the Széchenyi, Rudas and Lukács baths.
Good to know
Check the current opening status first: the bath is reported closed for refurbishment until 2028.
The Liberty Bridge and Gellért Hill (with the Citadella) are directly beside the building.
Széchenyi, Rudas and Lukács are the nearest alternatives if you want a thermal bath meanwhile.

historyIntro: The Gellért bathhouse is one of Budapest's grand Art Nouveau bathing landmarks, known as much for its architectural interiors as for its pools.

children.text: The bath developed around thermal springs on the Buda side of the Danube, combining ornate interiors with pools and wellness facilities. Its built setting forms part of Budapest's long spa tradition.
The operator announced a closure for major renovation beginning in October 2025. This attraction's historic significance does not mean it can currently be booked for bathing.

notice: Closed for renovation. The operator states that reopening is planned for 2028; this is not a confirmed booking date.

name: Széchenyi Thermal Bath
description: The Széchenyi Thermal Bath in City Park is a vast neo-Baroque bathing palace of indoor and outdoor pools fed by two thermal springs, open since 1913. It is one of the largest thermal bath complexes in Europe, set in the Városliget park.

children.text: The Széchenyi Thermal Bath opened in June 1913 and covers a total area of 6,220 square metres. It was designed by Győző Czigler, who died in 1905; construction began in 1909 under Ede Dvorák and Kálmán Gerster. The yellow neo-Baroque building, with its domes and courtyards, stands in City Park, close to Heroes' Square.

The baths are fed by two thermal springs. The first was reached by Vilmos Zsigmondy's artesian well, drilled between 1868 and 1878 in City Park, which found water at 74.5 °C at a depth of about 970 metres. A second spring, discovered in 1938 at a depth of roughly 1,240 to 1,256 metres (sources differ), supplies water at 77 °C. The bath was planned as the 'Artesian spa' and was named after István Széchenyi when it opened.

Today the complex has three outdoor and fifteen indoor pools, along with saunas and steam rooms. Outdoor pool temperatures range from 27 to 38 °C, and the indoor pools from 18 to 38 °C. The main swimming and thermal sections are open to men and women together.

The bath has been expanded over time: an extension designed by Imre Francsek Jr. was completed in 1927, a thermal section and a day hospital were added in the 1960s, and a full renovation ran from 1999 to 2009.
Good to know
Metro line 1 (the yellow Millennium Underground) stops at Széchenyi fürdő, right beside the entrance.
Ticket types, cabins and lockers, and opening hours vary: check the operator's website and book ahead in busy seasons.
Bring or hire a swimsuit, towel and flip-flops according to the ticket you choose.

historyIntro: Széchenyi Thermal Bath's yellow neo-Baroque buildings are part of a bathing tradition made possible by deep thermal-water exploration in City Park.

historySections.heading: From artesian drilling to grand bathhouse

children.text: The bath's roots reach back to the work of mining engineer Vilmos Zsigmondy, whose deep drilling revealed thermal waters beneath City Park. An earlier artesian bath was operating in the area by 1881.
The present Széchenyi complex opened in 1913 from plans by architect Győző Czigler. It was expanded in 1927 with outdoor bathing areas and went through further changes during the twentieth century.
